tur71-1: Why do people who stop exercising at home stop?
tur71-2: The reason is usually not a lack of willpower. In a systematic review of treatment adherence in physiotherapy, the factors shown by strong evidence to be linked with not keeping up exercise were: increased pain during exercise, low self-confidence, seeing many obstacles, little social support, anxiety, depression and a sense of helplessness.
tur71-3: Almost nothing. In a study that followed habit formation in real life, the time it took for a new behaviour to become automatic ranged from 18 to 254 days from person to person (median 66 days), and missing a single opportunity did not significantly affect the process.
tur71-4: The honest answer: useful, but not a miracle. In the latest Cochrane review, covering 139 trials and 12,468 people, exercise improved pain by about 13 points and daily function by about 12.5 points out of 100 at the end of the programme, compared with no treatment or usual care.
tur71-5: The certainty of the evidence is low to moderate, the effects were measured at the end of the programme, and the authors judged the clinical importance of this difference to be uncertain. That is why keeping going matters as much as starting.
tur71-6: According to the NICE guideline, in knee osteoarthritis morning stiffness is either absent or lasts no longer than 30 minutes. In people aged 45 and over, together with pain that increases with activity, the diagnosis is usually made by examination.
tur71-7: If you have new swelling, redness or warmth in your knee, or a fever
tur71-8: If your pain is getting steadily worse at rest or at night
tur71-9: In a study of around 20,000 people in England, those who spent at least 2 hours a week in nature were more likely than those with no nature contact to report good health and high wellbeing. This was a survey study; it shows an association, not cause and effect. It made no difference whether the 2 hours were spent in one go or spread out. Nature in Istanbul is closer than you think: parks, groves, the seaside and the waterfront all count.
tur71-10: The range where the positive association looked strongest; no extra gain was seen beyond it
tur71-11: You have reached 120 minutes. In the study, people who spent this much time in nature reported better health and wellbeing.
tur71-12: You are in the 200–300 minute range, where the positive association looked strongest in the study.
tur71-13: You are above 300 minutes. The study saw no further difference beyond this, but enjoy your time in nature.
tur71-14: 52 healthy older adults took a 15-minute walk once a week for 8 weeks. In the group asked to pay attention to the feeling of “awe” while walking – that sense of wonder in front of something far bigger than yourself – daily distress fell more, and emotions such as compassion and gratitude rose more, than in the group who walked without extra instructions. In the photos they took on their walks, they gradually gave less space to themselves and more to the scenery, and their smiles became more pronounced.
tur71-15: You were able to hold the tandem stance for 10 seconds; the situation the CDC treats as a sign of increased fall risk (less than 10 seconds) was not seen in this test. You can carry on with single-leg balance practice.
tur71-17: On a sturdy chair without arms, with your arms crossed over your chest, stand up and sit down at a controlled pace. If it feels hard, start by using your arms for support or with a higher chair.
tur71-18: No. In England, NICE’s 2025 guideline advises against using falls risk prediction tools to predict a person’s risk of falling; according to the guideline, gait and balance tests help to spot these problems but do not predict the risk of falling. So if you have fallen in the past year, tell your doctor whatever your result. If you have fallen more than once, were injured in a fall, lost consciousness or could not get up from the floor without help, you can ask for a comprehensive falls assessment.
